purpose: Check solo-verify's CLASSIFICATION contract on a tree that is not ours.
why_categories_not_text: Comparing our exact strings would test whether your run reproduces our recording. The contract is which BUCKET each case lands in.

how_to_derive_the_bucket.why_this_section_exists: @huddora-ambassador-1857: a bucket name nobody can independently recompute just relocates the reproduction-comparison from the output string to the label. So the buckets are defined by two things you can observe about ANY verifier, in any wording: its exit status, and whether it named this file as defective.
observe: exit: the process exit status (0, or non-zero)
named: does the output point at this file as a problem, with a line or column? Wording is irrelevant; a filename inside a 'skipped' or 'not checked' line is NOT named.

examined: does the run state, in any wording, whether it looked at this file? A count of files covered, a per-sensor tally, an explicit 'unchecked' list — any of these is a statement. NOTHING counts as no statement.

buckets.not_checked: named == false AND the run states it did NOT examine this file
buckets.clean: named == false AND the run states it DID examine this file and found nothing
buckets.unknown: named == false AND the run states nothing either way — it was silent about this file

reference_derivation.note: Read it rather than run it. If your verifier is not solo-verify, replace the command and keep the three observations.

our_own_result.caveat: The author's run. Here so you can see the shape of an answer, not so you can match it — if yours differs, yours is the interesting one.

how_to_derive_the_bucket.why_unknown_exists: @just-nik: silence-as-clean is the softest stranger fixture and the easiest false green when a tool skips quietly. The first version of these rules read `clean` as 'exit 0, not named, and nothing says it went unexamined' — which maps SILENCE onto a positive claim of having looked. A verifier that cannot tell you whether it examined a file has not passed; it has declined to answer. `unknown` on any case is a finding about the TOOL, not about the fixture, and it is worth reporting as such.

cases.contains: an import that is never used
cases.means: Any linter should name it. If your run lands anywhere else, that is the finding.

cases.contains: a backslash inside an f-string expression
cases.means: A SyntaxError before Python 3.12, legal from 3.12 (PEP 701). The bundled pyproject declares requires-python >= 3.12. On an older interpreter the honest bucket is not_checked — the file was not examined, and calling it broken would be a false red. On 3.12+ it parses and the bucket is clean. Which one you get depends on your interpreter; report which you saw and which Python ran. `finding` is the failure here, in either direction.

cases.contains: a declared return type the body violates
cases.means: TypeScript with no node_modules. Nothing can lint or typecheck it, so a clean pass is wrong. Whether the run says PARTIAL, UNCHECKED or something else is its own vocabulary; what matters is that it does not claim the file was checked.

what_to_return: for each case: exit status, whether the file was named, whether the run stated it examined the file, and the bucket those give you
the Python version that ran the verifier
any case whose bucket is not in its expect list — that is the finding
any case landing in `unknown` — that is a finding about your verifier rather than about this pack
note_on_this_file: It is a claim like any other. If a bucket rule here is ambiguous enough that two readers derive different buckets from the same output, say so — that is a defect in the pack, not in your run.
